action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right VP shunt catheter in place with normal ventricles (Evans index 0.27) and no sign of shunt malfunction; Fazekas 1 white matter foci; normal basal ganglia, midbrain and pons
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]; here it also shows whether the ventricles have enlarged behind the VP shunt

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sertraline flagged for serotonergic monitoring if an MAO-B inhibitor is added; amlodipine flagged for the standing blood pressure; no dopamine-blocking drug
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list for dopamine-blocking drugs and interactions before starting dopaminergic treatment
action_criteria.rationale: No dopamine-blocking drug is on his list, but sertraline bears on a later MAO-B inhibitor and amlodipine on the standing blood pressure during levodopa titration [Postuma_2015]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not attribute the parkinsonism to shunt failure or arrange shunt revision when the ventricles are normal on MRI and there is no headache, nausea or visual symptom
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): bradykinesia with right-hand rest tremor and rigidity, no absolute exclusion, no red flag; the response to levodopa may add a supportive criterion [Postuma_2015]
If the shunt valve is programmable, check its setting after the MRI and reset it if the magnet has changed it

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months [NICE_NG71]
If a dopamine agonist is used, warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness and ask about them at every visit [NICE_NG71]
Refer for physiotherapy for gait initiation, turning and balance (three near-falls on turns), and for speech and language therapy for the hypophonia

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic confusion: EEG does not inform this parkinsonism
The ventricles are normal on MRI and there is no inflammatory or infectious feature: a lumbar CSF study or tap test has no role here
No murmur, heart failure or cardiac symptom: an echocardiogram does not inform the parkinsonism
The near-falls occur on turning, without light-headedness or loss of consciousness: rhythm monitoring is not indicated
No cardiac symptom, syncope or QT-prolonging drug planned: an ECG does not inform the parkinsonism
DaT SPECT is indicated when tremor cannot be clinically separated from parkinsonism; here the clinical diagnosis is clear and the scan would not change management [NICE_NG71]
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic measurement suffices

differential.diagnosis: Parkinsonism from shunt failure with recurrent obstructive hydrocephalus
differential.key_features: Prior VP shunt for aqueductal stenosis, but the MRI shows normal ventricles (Evans index 0.27) with the catheter in place, he has no headache, nausea or visual change, and the syndrome is an asymmetric rest-tremor parkinsonism
Rest tremor with re-emergence, no action tremor, and bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity, which ET does not cause
No antipsychotic or dopamine-blocking antiemetic exposure; sertraline does not cause an asymmetric rest-tremor parkinsonism
Asymmetric upper-limb onset with rest tremor; only punctate Fazekas 1 white matter foci and normal basal ganglia on MRI
No orthostatic symptoms, urinary urgency or cerebellar signs; rest tremor; normal putamina and pons on MRI
MoCA 27/30 without functional decline, no fluctuations or visual hallucinations, no dream enactment (sleep talking only)

key_clinical_evidence: Right-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz pill-rolling rest tremor of the right hand that re-emerges on posture, with micrographia and hypophonia: parkinsonism with one supportive criterion (rest tremor) and no red flag [Postuma_2015]
No levodopa trial yet and no validated smell test, so the supportive criteria are not two: clinically probable PD [Postuma_2015]
MRI with normal ventricles (Evans index 0.27), the shunt catheter in place and no sign of shunt malfunction: the shunt history does not explain the parkinsonism
Near-falls only on turns and in doorways, pull test with two steps and self-correction, full vertical gaze: no early-falls or gaze red flag

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Shunt failure would enlarge the ventricles and cause headache, nausea or a gait apraxia; the MRI shows normal ventricles with the catheter in place, and the asymmetric rest-tremor parkinsonism is PD
red_herrings.data_point: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to idiopathic aqueductal stenosis, treated with a right ventriculoperitoneal shunt in 2016
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward shunt malfunction or chronic hydrocephalic gait

interactions: Sertraline with an MAO-B inhibitor: serotonin syndrome is rare; use the lowest dose and monitor. Fluoxetine and fluvoxamine are best avoided with rasagiline.

Amlodipine lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
warnings: Metformin and aspirin: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.
High-protein meals can reduce levodopa absorption; distribute protein evenly through the day.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Chen is a 62-year-old right-handed retired engineer who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic with an 18-month history of progressive right-sided tremor, stiffness, and difficulty with fine motor tasks. He has a past medical history notable for obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to idiopathic aqueductal stenosis, which was treated with a right ventriculoperitoneal shunt approximately 10 years ago with complete resolution of his hydrocephalus symptoms. He was followed with serial imaging after the shunt placement; the last surveillance scan was 3 years ago, before the current symptoms began.

Approximately 18 months ago, the patient's wife first noticed that his right hand would shake intermittently while he was watching television in the evening. The tremor was initially subtle and sporadic, occurring primarily when his hand was at rest in his lap, and the patient himself was not particularly concerned. Over the following months, the tremor became more persistent and noticeable, particularly during periods of rest or when walking. He reports that the shaking diminishes or stops completely when he deliberately uses his right hand to pick up objects or perform tasks, but it returns shortly after he relaxes.

Over the past year, Mr. Chen has experienced increasing difficulty with activities that require manual dexterity. He is an avid calligrapher and has noticed that his brush strokes have become progressively smaller and less controlled, with the characters becoming cramped and illegible toward the end of a line. He has difficulty buttoning his shirt, particularly the top buttons, and his wife now assists him each morning. He reports that shaving with his right hand has become notably slower, and he sometimes nicks himself because of the tremor.

In the past six to eight months, both the patient and his wife have noticed changes in his walking. His wife describes that he shuffles his feet when starting to walk, particularly after sitting for prolonged periods, and that his right arm no longer swings naturally at his side. He has had three near-fall episodes in the past four months, all occurring during turns or when navigating through doorways, though he has not fallen to the ground. He denies any loss of consciousness, lightheadedness, or vertigo associated with these episodes. His wife has also observed that his facial expressions have become less animated and that his voice has become softer over the past year, requiring her to ask him to repeat himself frequently.

The patient denies visual hallucinations, vivid dreams, or acting out dreams during sleep, though his wife reports that he occasionally talks in his sleep. He denies difficulty swallowing or drooling. He reports mild constipation over the past year, managed with increased dietary fiber. He denies urinary urgency or incontinence. He has not been exposed to antipsychotic medications, antiemetics such as metoclopramide, or other dopamine-blocking agents. There is no history of encephalitis, repeated head trauma, or exposure to environmental toxins including pesticides or heavy metals. His shunt has been functioning well, and he denies any recurrence of headaches, nausea, or visual changes that would suggest shunt malfunction.

neurological_exam.additional: Resting tremor observed in the right hand at approximately 4-5 Hz, with a classic pill-rolling quality, most prominent when the patient is seated with hands in his lap and during ambulation. Tremor suppresses with intentional movement and re-emerges after a brief latency when holding posture (re-emergent tremor). Mild intermittent rest tremor in the right foot. No action tremor. No head or voice tremor. Handwriting sample demonstrates progressive micrographia with a tendency for the characters to become increasingly cramped and smaller across the page. Glabellar tap sign positive with failure to habituate after 12 taps.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing without dysmetria bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements reveal progressive decrement in speed and amplitude of finger tapping and hand pronation-supination on the right, with clear fatiguing and halting after 8-10 repetitions. Left side shows mild slowing but maintains amplitude. Heel-to-shin testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally (3 mm to 2 mm). Extraocular movements full in all directions without restriction. No vertical gaze palsy. Facial sensation intact to light touch and pinprick bilaterally. Marked hypomimia with reduced spontaneous blinking (approximately 8 blinks per minute). Facial movements symmetric but diminished in amplitude. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait notable for markedly reduced right arm swing. Mildly shortened stride length with shuffling on initiation and when approaching doorways. Forward-flexed posture of approximately 15 degrees. Turns require 5-6 small steps (en bloc turning). No festination observed. Pull test shows two steps of retropulsion but self-corrects without assistance. Tandem gait mildly impaired. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech is hypophonic with reduced prosody but fluent and coherent. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Montreal Cognitive Assessment score 27/30, losing one point on trail-making B, one on phonemic fluency and one on delayed recall (word retrieved with a category cue). Affect mildly blunted but appropriate. No evidence of hallucinations or psychosis.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Increased tone in the right upper extremity with prominent cogwheel rigidity at the wrist and elbow, augmented by contralateral activation maneuver. Left upper extremity shows mild rigidity at the wrist only. Lower extremity tone mildly increased bilaterally, right greater than left. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No pyramidal signs.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, proprioception, and vibration intact in all extremities. No dermatomal sensory loss. No cortical sensory deficits.
